name: Haisla
confidence_why: Janzen 2023 derives Haisla stress from syllable weight (leftmost long vowel, else leftmost full vowel, else the final syllable) and Baleno, Janzen & Yoder 2024 confirm it acoustically, with Bach 1990 and Wilson 1987 agreeing that stress is largely predictable apart from lexically accented suffixes, but Vink 1977 presents minimal pairs and calls stress phonemic, and the fullest description, Lincoln & Rath 1986, remains unchecked.

catalog_quote: This analysis shows that word-stress in this language is fully predictable. As in all other North Wakashan languages, there is a strong preference for assigning word-stress to the leftmost syllable. Complicating this, however, is the presence of long vowels in x̄a’iselak̓ala: /aa, uu, ii, ai, au/. ... I analyse this language as being moraic based, that is, syllables with morae attract stress. The underlying vowels /a, u, i/ are moraic (µ). A schwa vowel followed by a resonant syllable coda /ən., əm., əl., əy., əw./ are also moraic. Schwa alone as a syllable nucleus is not moraic at all. The leftmost of these are assigned word-stress. ... I treat long vowels as heavy syllables, or as bimoraic (µµ). ... In each case, the heavy syllable will supersede the more regular leftmost stress rule pervasive in North Wakashan languages. ... when there is more than one heavy syllable within the same …

tone_statements.quote: A HE vocalic plain resonant that is neither preceded nor followed by another one has either high tone indicated by an acute, or low tone indicated by its absence, cf. HE /k̓ʷás/ 'mussel' versus HE /k̓ʷas/ 'sit on the ground outside'. The other isolects have accent instead. In HA it is free and to be indicated whenever not automatic, in this paper by the prime symbol before the accent bearer. Thus, HA /ƛ'ix̌əzu/ 'board for beating time' but HA /c̓xa/ 'to singe'. … Vocalic glottalized resonants never have HE high tone or distinctive HA/OO accent.
tone_statements.summary: No tone in Haisla: Heiltsuk high/low tone corresponds to a free accent in Haisla, often on the first vocalic plain resonant (Oowekyala pattern), sometimes word-final; placement awaits further study.

readall_conflicts: The one listed work (Lincoln & Rath 1986) could not be opened, so no conflict can be stated for it. Among the Haisla sources already held by the project in our check folder (downloaded 2026-09-16, not part of this task's work list), Vink 1977 ('A Haisla phonology', ICSNL 12, sec. 0.5, printed p. 115) says stress on the first syllable 'can by no means be given as a general rule, as a considerable amount of the items in the lexicon has middle or final stress', i.e. treats placement as lexical; Wilson 1987 (BLS 13, p. 326) says Haisla stress/pitch 'is not nearly so regular' as Nootkan or Kwak'wala and that some speakers replace stress with a HLH pitch pattern in connected discourse; Baleno, Janzen & Yoder 2024 (ICSNL 59, pp. 14-15) reconcile these as an ordered system: lexically stressed suffixes first, otherwise leftmost heavy (bimoraic) syllable, otherwise leftmost moraic syllable, otherwise (no moraic syllable) the final syllable, noting that the earlier authors did not take phonemic vowel length into account. So the older 'unpredictable' descriptions versus the 2024 weight-based analysis is the only disagreement, and the 2024 paper explains it as an analytical gap rather than a factual one.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every segment of the deciding quote, domain quote and exceptions quote is verbatim in the Janzen 2023 PDF we hold at the stated pages (188, 189, 191, 192, 194-195, 196, 198). (2) Deciding source: an 11-pp ICSNL working paper (2023) devoted to Haisla stress from recent fieldwork; kind = phonology article. sources.citation: Baleno, Grace, Jonathan Janzen & Brendon Yoder. 2024. Acoustic Correlates of Word Stress in Haisla. In D. K. E. Reisinger et al. (eds.), Papers for ICSNL 59, 14-23. Vancouver: UBCWPL.
sources.quote: 'Haisla typically assigns stress like other North Wakashan languages to the leftmost stress-bearing (moraic) syllable, or applies the default-to-opposite rule if the word contains no moraic syllable... (1) Assign stress to a lexically stressed syllable. (2) Assign stress to the leftmost heavy (bimoraic) syllable. (3) If no syllable is bimoraic, assign stress to the leftmost moraic syllable. (4) If no syllable contains a mora, assign stress to the rightmost syllable.' tone.quote: The acute mark, as in á , is written over a vowel or other main part of a syllable to show that that syllable is stressed or accented. Many Haisla speakers go down in pitch, rather than up on the stressed syllable. Compare these pairs of words: hím̓as `chief, king' him̓áas `chiefs' málhela `to swim' malheláa `to do things in pairs, together with someone'

tone.quote: Likewise, Haisla, another Kwakiutlan language, appears to have developed a pitch accent (Lincoln & Rath 1980). The accent generally appears to fall where the general stress rules would predict main stress, but the mapping is far from perfect. However, nothing in the Haisla data would argue against taking the Xwakwala rule as basic.
